paragraphs.text: Saltwell has one pump and the pump is dying. For three weeks the handle has brought up less water each morning, and now it coughs air by noon. The town council, which is four people and a dog, has pooled what coin it has and hired you. Somewhere east of the wet branch of the Dry Fork stands the old company pumphouse. Its governor valve, if it still exists, would set the Saltwell pump right. Bring it back before the trough goes dry.

A board nailed to the fence post reads SALTWELL, POPULATION ENOUGH. Someone has scratched out ENOUGH and written FEWER. Below it, in fresher paint, a second board lists the town rules. No shooting inside the fence. No drinking from the trough before the animals. No credit at the store. The paint on the last rule is the thickest.

The dry goods store smells of lamp oil and dust. Shelves run to the ceiling, though most of them hold empty jars kept for the day there is something to put in them. The owner watches you from behind a counter worn pale by elbows. A slate by the door says rounds come six to a box and are sold one box at a time.

The pump handle moves with a dry rasp. A thin dribble wets the trough and stops. Underneath the head a gap shows where the governor valve should sit; someone has jammed a carved wooden plug in its place, and the plug is splitting. Nothing here will hold for long without the real part from the pumphouse across the wet branch.

A woman with rolled sleeves and a wet cloth over one shoulder looks up from a cot. Bottles stand in rows on a plank shelf, each labelled in a careful hand. She sets bones, stitches cuts and asks for payment up front, because, as she puts it, patients who wake up fixed have short memories.

A lean woman leans on a rifle by the well road, watching the gate as if she expects it to move. She says her name is Orla Penn and that she has walked the Dry Fork more times than the riverbed has flooded. She heard about the pump. She will ride with you to the pumphouse and back for a share of whatever the council pays, and she will keep watch at night without being asked.

A leaning signpost stands where the track from Saltwell nears the gravel of the old river. One arm points north-east and reads NINEMILE. A second arm, newer, points south-east and reads PUMPHOUSE, CLOSED. A third arm once pointed somewhere else, but only a nail remains. The wind has sanded the letters so thin you read them partly by touch.

Three figures rise from behind the bridge rail with scarves over their faces and guns already up. One of them calls out that the bridge costs whatever you carry, payable now. The plank bridge is the only dry crossing of the wet branch for miles, and they know it. Nobody waits for an answer.

The plank bridge sways under your boots. Someone has carved tally marks into the rail, dozens of them, and nailed a hand-drawn map to the last post with the bridge circled in charcoal. The water below moves slowly south, dark and quiet. On the far bank the road climbs toward land the Saltwell council has not seen in years.

Ninemile is a wide street and two rows of adobe buildings that have outlived whatever business built them. A gunsmith's sign hangs on the north side and an outfitter's on the far corner. People here keep their hats low and their voices lower. A storehouse at the east end has a new padlock on an old door, which in Ninemile counts as news.

Racks of long guns line the gunsmith's back wall, most of them missing a part. The smith files a spring at the bench without looking up. A card nailed to the counter reads REPAIRS IN THREE DAYS, ROUNDS TODAY. Behind him a door stands open on a yard where tin cans hang from a wire, every one of them holed.

The padlock gives with a click and the hasp swings free. Inside, the storehouse holds crates of rusted fittings, a broken cart axle and a desk with one drawer. In the drawer lies a punched steel card stamped with the old pumping company's mark, the kind that once opened company gates. Someone in Ninemile has been keeping it safe or keeping it hidden.

A broad man in a grease-black apron sits on an upturned bucket, taking apart a clock with a bent nail. He introduces himself as Teodor Lusk, mechanic, and says he worked at the pumphouse as a boy before the company left. He remembers the consoles and the gates and roughly where the spare parts were kept. He wants to see it again, and he wants paying.

Wren Abara sits on the outfitter's counter with her boots on a crate of bandages. She is quick, quiet and openly unimpressed. She has crossed the beetle flats twice and come back both times, which she says is the only qualification that counts. She will join a party whose leader can talk her into it, and she makes it plain that this is hard.

The long room was a dining hall once. Benches are stacked against the walls and the counter at the back holds a row of clean, empty cups. An old man sweeping the floor tells you, without being asked, that the pumphouse crawlers sleep in the cool of the main corridor and wake when they hear boots on concrete. He sweeps around your feet and says no more.

The dry fork of the river runs north-west here, a broad bed of rounded stones with not a drop between them. Old flood marks stain a boulder higher than your head. Your boots find a rusted length of pipe half buried in the gravel, stamped with the same company mark you saw on the signpost. The company ran water through here once.

You find the shallow line where the stones lie close to the surface and cross with the water at your knees. The current is stronger than it looks and cold enough to ache. On the far bank you stamp the water out of your boots. The stones you set in place behind you will make the crossing easier next time.

Concrete steps lead down into the dark under the rock hump. The air at the bottom is cool and smells of wet iron. A painted arrow on the wall points down the corridor toward a word too faded to read. Somewhere far ahead, a drip lands in standing water at a slow, steady count.

Something moves in the corridor ahead, low and many-legged, and then there are four of them: pale crawling things the size of dogs, with plated backs and pincers that click on the concrete. They have made a nest of rags and wire in the cool of the passage, and they come at you all at once.

The console screen warms from black to green. Most of the switches do nothing, but one row still answers, and with a heavy clunk somewhere below, a gate on the lower corridor slides open. Text crawls across the screen listing maintenance stores that no longer exist. The last line reads SPARES CAGE UNLOCKED, which is the only good news it has.

The steel gate rattles in its frame as the lock box reads the card. A green lamp you had not noticed blinks once, and the bars slide aside with a long scrape. Beyond lies the governor chamber, where the main pump once ran. The floor is dry, and footprints in the dust show nobody has been through in years.

The great pump stands silent in the middle of the chamber, taller than two men. A rack along the wall holds spare parts in labelled slots, most of them empty. One slot still holds a brass valve the size of a fist, wrapped in waxed cloth. The label beneath it reads GOVERNOR, SALTWELL LINE, in a hand that took care over it.

A big man with a split lip sits in the corner of the spares cage, surrounded by empty tins. He says his name is Sallow Kett and that he came down here looking for copper and got shut in when the gate jammed. That was eleven days ago, by his count of the tins. He will carry anything, hit anything and follow you anywhere with daylight in it.

The valve seats with a soft click and the pump handle comes up heavy. Then water, cold and clean, gushes into the trough until it spills over the lip and darkens the street. People come out of every door in Saltwell. The council, all four of them and the dog, stand at the front. Someone starts counting the coins they owe you, and nobody minds that the count takes a long time.
